cards.explanation: The answer is Jerusalem, friends. Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar's father and the earlier king of Babylon, took those vessels from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem (Daniel 5:3). These weren't just fancy cups. They came from God's house, and that matters for everything coming next.

The answer is so they can drink from them. The text says Belshazzar gave the order “…so that the king could drink from them, along with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines.” Belshazzar, Babylon's king, wanted vessels from God's house as party cups. The text also says he gave the order under the influence of the wine, and I think that tells you how the evening is going.

The answer is True. The text says that as they drank the wine, “…they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone.” They were doing it with vessels from the house of God in Jerusalem. Keep that picture in your head, friends, because Daniel talks about it later (Daniel 5:23).

The answer is that his face grows pale and his knees knock together. The text says “…his face grew pale and his thoughts so alarmed him that his hips gave way and his knees knocked together.” A moment ago, Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was drinking wine with his nobles. Then the fingers of a hand started writing on his wall, and his knees did the knocking.

The answer is the wise men of Babylon. The text says the king called for the enchanters, astrologers and diviners, and it names them “…these wise men of Babylon…” Belshazzar, Babylon's king, went straight to the experts he already had. You'd call your own experts first too, friends.

The answer is that they could neither read it nor interpret it. They got NOTHING. The text says all the king's wise men came in, “…but they could not read the inscription or interpret it for him.” That's all of them, not just a couple. I think a thousand nobles watching that happen is a whole lot of quiet.

The answer is False. The text says that after the wise men came up empty, “…King Belshazzar became even more terrified, his face grew even more pale, and his nobles were bewildered.” He was already scared, and now he's scared on top of scared. His nobles were bewildered right along with him.

The answer is King Nebuchadnezzar. The queen says, “Your father, King Nebuchadnezzar, appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners.” Nebuchadnezzar is Belshazzar's father, the king who took the temple vessels. She reminds Belshazzar that his own father was the one who appointed this man.

The answer is that Daniel will give him the interpretation. The queen tells the king, “Summon Daniel, therefore, and he will give you the interpretation.” The room is full of outcry, and she walks in with one name. I think that's one calm queen.

The answer is False. Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah, says to the king, “You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else.” The purple and the gold chain were on the table, and Daniel pushed them back across it. Plenty of people would've said yes, friends.

The answer is that he will read the inscription and interpret it. Daniel says, “Nevertheless, I will read the inscription for the king and interpret it for him.” He turns down the gifts, but he doesn't turn down the job. Both things are in the same breath.

The answer is that he was deposed from his throne. Daniel says that when Nebuchadnezzar's heart became arrogant and his spirit was hardened with pride, “…he was deposed from his royal throne, and his glory was taken from him.” Daniel is telling this to Nebuchadnezzar's son, Belshazzar, so he's reminding the king of his own family's history. Pride cost Nebuchadnezzar a lot.

The answer is False, friends. Daniel tells Belshazzar, “But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this.” Just before that, Daniel told how Nebuchadnezzar was driven away from mankind until he acknowledged that the Most High God rules (Daniel 5:21). Belshazzar knew his father's story, and he still didn't humble his heart.

The answer is that He holds the king's very breath in His hand. Daniel describes Him as “…the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways.” That's the true God, the one Belshazzar didn't glorify. The gods Belshazzar praised “…cannot see or hear or understand.” and the God Daniel names holds the king's breath.

The answer is False. Daniel says, “Therefore He sent the hand that wrote the inscription.” He is talking about the Lord of heaven, whom Belshazzar did not glorify (Daniel 5:23). The writing didn't come from the gods Belshazzar praised.

The answer is that God has numbered the days of his reign. Daniel says, “MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end.” Notice who's doing the counting: God. Daniel says it right to Belshazzar's face, and I think that takes nerve.

The word is deficient. Daniel says, “TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient.” Belshazzar was weighed, and he came up short. Daniel read that word out right in front of the king.

The answer is the Medes. Daniel says, “PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.” That's the third part of the message, and it's about the kingdom itself. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was hearing that his kingdom was going to someone else.

The answer is True. The text says, “Then Belshazzar gave the command, and they clothed Daniel in purple, placed a gold chain around his neck, and proclaimed him the third highest ruler in the kingdom.” Belshazzar had just heard that his reign was ending, and he kept his promise anyway. I think that's a king keeping his word on a very strange night.

The answer is Darius the Mede. The text says, “…Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.” Belshazzar was slain that very night (Daniel 5:30). Daniel had read PERES as the kingdom divided and given over to the Medes and Persians (Daniel 5:28).
